working_title: Book-building: how an IPO's price is set
audience_one_line: Someone who keeps seeing a 'price band' on every IPO and wants to understand what it is, why there's a range instead of one price, who actually decides the final number, and how long they have to apply.
must_answer: What book-building is, in plain terms: the company doesn't fix one price up front; it publishes a range (a price band) and lets demand from investors over a few days settle the final price. Contrast briefly with a fixed-price issue.

What the price band is and the hard limits on it: the cap cannot exceed 120% of the floor, and must be at least 105% of the floor; the floor cannot be below the share's face value; the band must be advertised at least two working days before the issue opens.

How long an IPO stays open: at least three and at most ten working days; what happens if the band is revised (window extends by at least three working days) or there's a force-majeure event (at least one extra day).

The minimum you can apply for: the minimum application value is set between ₹10,000 and ₹15,000, and applications come in multiples of that lot; at least 25% of the issue price is payable on application, but the full amount for an offer for sale.
Who underwrites and runs the book: the lead manager (merchant banker) is appointed and compulsorily underwrites the issue; the draft red herring prospectus deliberately omits the price.
The basic floor on a valid issue: an allotment cannot happen with fewer than 1,000 prospective allottees, and QIB/employee allotment is proportionate.
must_not_say: Investment advice — whether to bid at the cap, whether a band is 'cheap' or 'expensive', how to time an application.
Predictions about specific IPO pricing or demand.
Detailed cut-off-price retail bidding mechanics unless grounded in the corpus — do not assert market-practice details the regulation excerpts don't support.
Anything about post-listing price movement — that belongs to the listing-day article.
Any number, percentage, or rule not present in the source excerpts.
angle: Explain why an IPO shows a price range instead of a price, and who turns that range into a single number. Lead with the plain idea — book-building means the price is discovered from demand, not declared in advance — then ground the specifics in the actual ICDR limits: the 105%-to-120% band, the face-value floor, the two-day advertisement, the three-to-ten-day window, the ₹10,000–15,000 lot. The reader should come away knowing exactly what the band on a live IPO means and what constrains it.
notes: Third article. Tests the explain-first pipeline on a mechanics topic with a fresh single source harvested from the cached ICDR PDF. Voice: explain-then-ground (the live what-is-an-ipo voice), not the detector-experiment register.
